data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

The pyramids get the attention. The interesting question is duller and bigger: why did the first cities show up on rivers, in several parts of the world, without those people ever meeting?

1. Read **Follow the Food, Find the City**.
2. Learn the words in **Nile Words**, then win the **Crossword**.
3. Study the **From Flood to City** chart — it is the whole argument on one page.
4. Trace **The Chain** concept map before you take the quiz.
5. Sort the cards in **Cause or Effect?**
6. Take **Nile Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Chain**.
8. Read **Egypt Questions Kids Ask** — one answer will annoy you.
9. Finish with **Investigation: What the Record Leaves Out**.

Your job this week: notice one thing you use that only exists because somebody else grows the food. 🌾

history.title: Follow the Food, Find the City
history.data:
## Follow the Food, Find the City

Egypt is mostly desert. Almost nobody lived in the desert. Nearly everyone lived in a green strip a few miles wide, along one river.

The Greek writer Herodotus called Egypt the gift of the Nile. He was close, though the gift needed a lot of work.

Each year the **Nile** flooded. The water spread across the low ground and left behind dark **silt**, a fine mud carried down from highlands far to the south. Silt is rich. Crops grow in it. And unlike most floods, this one arrived at roughly the same time each year, so people could plan around it.

Here is the chain that follows, and it is the reason this lesson exists.

Predictable floods meant reliable farming. Reliable farming meant a **surplus** — more grain than the farmers themselves needed. A surplus sounds boring. It is the most important idea here.

Once there is extra food, some people do not have to farm. They can spend their days doing one thing instead. Those are **specialists**: potters, weavers, builders, priests, soldiers. **Specialization** is only possible when somebody else grows your dinner.

Specialists need organizing, and grain needs counting. So Egyptians developed **hieroglyphs**, a writing system, and much of the earliest writing anywhere is not poetry. It is receipts. Lists of grain. Records of who owed what.

Writing and stored grain made a **bureaucracy** possible: officials, taxes, and a **pharaoh** at the top who claimed to be both king and god.

Now the part worth arguing about. We know this story mostly from tombs, temples, and official records, which were made by and for the powerful. The farmers who made the surplus possible left almost nothing behind. **Archaeologists** work hard on ordinary settlements to fill that gap, and much is still unknown.

So the pyramids are real, and they are not the point. Follow the food, and you find the city.

history.title: Nile Check

questions.question: What made the Nile's flood so useful to farmers?
options: It was larger than any other river flood on Earth
It arrived at about the same time each year, so people could plan
It washed the old soil away and left clean sand behind
It happened only once in a farmer's lifetime, so it did no harm
questions.correctAnswer: It arrived at about the same time each year, so people could plan

questions.question: Why is a surplus the hinge of the whole chain?
options: It let some people stop farming and do one thing instead
It meant farmers could finally eat as much as they wanted
It made the soil richer for the following year's planting
It was the first thing the pharaoh ever asked people for
questions.correctAnswer: It let some people stop farming and do one thing instead

questions.question: Much of the earliest writing anywhere is best described as what?
options: Poems and stories about gods and heroes
Letters written between distant family members
Records and receipts: lists of grain and who owed what
Instructions carved to teach children their letters
questions.correctAnswer: Records and receipts: lists of grain and who owed what

questions.question: Why do historians say the record of ancient Egypt is lopsided?
options: Most of it was written in a language nobody can read
Egyptians deliberately destroyed the records of farmers
Almost all of it was found in the last twenty years
Tombs and official records were made by and for the powerful
questions.correctAnswer: Tombs and official records were made by and for the powerful

questions.question: A specialist in ancient Egypt could exist only because ______.
options: the pharaoh personally chose them for the work
somebody else was growing enough food for them
they had learned to read and write hieroglyphs
the flood had failed and farming became pointless
questions.correctAnswer: somebody else was growing enough food for them

questions.question: Explain the chain from the Nile's flood to the first officials, in order, naming each link.
questions.expectedAnswer: The flood arrived predictably and left rich silt, so farming was reliable. Reliable farming produced a surplus of grain. The surplus freed some people from farming to become specialists. Stored grain had to be counted, so writing appeared, and records made officials, taxes and a bureaucracy possible.

questions.question: A classmate says we know ancient Egypt well because so much survived. What is the problem with that?
questions.expectedAnswer: What survived is mostly tombs, temples and official records, which were made by and for the powerful. The farmers who made the surplus possible left almost nothing, so the record tells us far more about rulers than about ordinary people, and much is still unknown.

reflections.text: Name one thing you used today that only exists because somebody else grows food.

history.title: Egypt Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Were the pyramids built by slaves? ⛏️
data.answer: The old story says yes. The evidence says mostly no. Workers' villages near Giza show bread ovens, medical care and burials of honour. Most builders appear to have been paid labourers, many working in the flood season when fields were underwater. Egypt did hold enslaved people, so it is not a clean story either.

data.question: Did the same thing happen anywhere else?
data.answer: Yes, and that is the striking part. Mesopotamia, the Indus valley and China all grew early cities on rivers, and none of them copied the others. The same conditions produced the same chain more than once.

data.question: How do we read hieroglyphs? 🪨
data.answer: For centuries nobody could. The Rosetta Stone carried the same message in three scripts, and by working from the known Greek, scholars broke the rest. Champollion published the key in 1822.

data.question: Why is Egypt so dry if it has a huge river?
data.answer: Almost no rain falls there. The water is entirely the river's, carried in from wetter highlands far to the south. Step a few miles from the bank and you are in desert.

data.question: Was the pharaoh really thought to be a god?
data.answer: Officially yes, and Egyptians took the claim seriously. Whether ordinary farmers believed it as fully as the temples said is exactly the kind of question the surviving record cannot answer.

data.question: What happened when the flood failed? 🌾
data.answer: Hunger, and sometimes worse. Low floods are linked to periods of unrest and to the collapse of central rule. The whole chain rested on the river, which makes it strong and also fragile.

history.title: Investigation: What the Record Leaves Out
history.meta: 6th Grade • Investigation brief • read a source for its silences

data.title: What the Record Leaves Out
data.instructions: Take one thing that survived from ancient Egypt. Work out what it tells you, what it cannot tell you, and who it leaves out.
data.fitReason: The standard asks students to detect limitations in the historical record. Doing that on one real object beats being told the record is biased, because the student has to find the silence themselves.

brief.context: Your class has images and descriptions of several surviving sources: a tomb painting of a harvest, a scribe's grain tally, a pyramid, a worker's village bread oven, and a temple wall listing a pharaoh's victories. Each team takes one.
brief.audience: The rest of the class, who will build a shared list of what the record can and cannot show
brief.drivingQuestion: What does this one source let us claim with confidence, what can it only hint at, and whose life does it leave out entirely?
brief.seedDirection: Ask who made it, who paid for it, and who it was meant to impress. The answer to those three usually explains the silences.
lockedLessonFacts: We know this story mostly from tombs, temples and official records.
Those were made by and for the powerful.
The farmers who made the surplus possible left almost nothing behind.
Archaeologists dig ordinary settlements to fill the gap, and much is still unknown.
openQuestions: Who made this source, and for whom?
What would it have cost to make, and who could afford that?
What would you need to find, to check a claim this source makes?
stakeholders: The class building the shared list
Your team, who must agree on the confidence rating
The people the source leaves out
criteria: Three claims the source supports, each rated strong, likely or unsure with a reason
One claim the source appears to make that it cannot actually prove
A named group whose life this source does not show, and why not
At least four glossary words used correctly
constraints: No claim without a reason attached to it
brief.deliverable: A one-page source report: what it is, three rated claims, one claim it cannot prove, and the group it leaves out — plus the single piece of evidence you would most want to find next.

parallelExample.context: A team took the temple wall listing a pharaoh's victories.
parallelExample.move: They rated the fact of the campaign as likely, the size of the enemy army as unsure, and the total victory as weak, because the wall was paid for by the man it praises and no defeat was ever carved.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: They separated what happened from what the source wanted people to believe, using who paid for it as the test.
